{{Short description|Marking an argument as obvious or trivial}}
{{distinguish|Argumentum ad baculum}}
{{redirect|Proof by verbosity|the repetition-related fallacy|Proof by assertion|the ceaseless-argument fallacy|argumentum ad nauseam}}
'''Proof by intimidation''' (or ''argumentum verbosum'') is a humorous phrase used mainly in [[mathematics]] to refer to a specific form of [[hand-waving]] whereby one attempts to advance an argument by giving an argument loaded with jargon and obscure results or by marking it as obvious or [[Triviality (mathematics)|trivial]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bennett |first=Bo |url=https://www.logicallyfallacious.com/tools/lp/Bo/LogicalFallacies/144/Proof-by-Intimidation |title=Proof by Intimidation |website=logicallyfallacious.com |access-date=2019-12-01}}</ref> It attempts to intimidate the audience into simply accepting the result without evidence by appealing to their ignorance or lack of understanding.<ref>
{{cite journal |title=Cogno-Intellectualism, Rhetorical Logic, and the Craske-Trump Theorem |url=http://www.es.ele.tue.nl/~tbasten/fun/rhetoric_logic.pdf |author=Michael H. F. Wilkinson |journal=[[Annals of Improbable Research]] |volume=6 |issue=5 |pages=15–16 |access-date=2008-02-22}}</ref>

The phrase is often used when the author is an authority in their field, presenting their proof to people who respect [[A priori and a posteriori|''a priori'']] the author's insistence of the validity of the proof, while in other cases, the author might simply claim that their statement is true because it is trivial or because they say so. Usage of this phrase is for the most part in good humour, though it can also appear in serious criticism.<ref>
{{cite journal
|title=Richard Feynman and computation
|url=https://cds.cern.ch/record/411350/files/p101.pdf
|author=Tony Hey
|journal= Contemporary Physics
|volume=40
|issue=4
|pages=257–265
|year=1999
|access-date=2008-02-22
|doi=10.1080/001075199181459|bibcode=1999ConPh..40..257H
}}
</ref> A proof by intimidation is often associated with phrases such as:
* "Clearly..."
* "It is self-evident that..."
* "It can be easily shown that..."
* "... does not warrant a proof."
* "The proof is left as an exercise for the reader."
* "It is trivial..."

Outside mathematics, "proof by intimidation" is also cited by critics of [[junk science]], to describe cases in which [[scientific evidence]] is thrown aside in favour of dubious arguments {{Ndash}} such as those presented to the public by articulate advocates who pose as experts in their field.<ref>
{{cite journal |title=Junk science: Appearances can be deceiving |author=Marjorie K. Jeffcoat |journal=[[Journal of the American Dental Association]] |volume=134 |pages=802–803 |date=July 2003 |pmid=12892436 |issue=7 |doi=10.14219/jada.archive.2003.0268}}
</ref>

Proof by intimidation may also back valid assertions. [[Ronald A. Fisher]] claimed in the book credited with the new evolutionary synthesis, "...by the analogy of compound interest the present value of the future offspring of persons aged ''x'' is easily seen to be...", thence presenting a novel integral-laden definition of [[reproductive value (population genetics)|reproductive value]].<ref name="Fisher 1930 p. 27">{{cite book |last=Fisher |first=Ronald Aylmer |title=The genetical theory of natural selection |publisher=The Clarendon Press |publication-place=Oxford |year=1930 |oclc=18500548 |page=27}}</ref> At this, Hal Caswell remarked, "With all due respect to Fisher, I have yet to meet anyone who finds this equation 'easily seen.{{' "}}<ref name="Caswell 2001 p. 92">{{cite book |last=Caswell |first=Hal |title=Matrix Population Models |publisher=Sinauer Associates, Incorporated |date=2001 |isbn=0-87893-096-5 |page=92}}</ref> Valid proofs were provided by subsequent researchers such as [[Leo A. Goodman]] (1968).<ref name="Goodman 1968 pp. 382–409">{{cite journal |last=Goodman |first=Leo A. |title=An elementary approach to the population projection-matrix, to the population reproductive value, and to related topics in the mathematical theory of population growth |journal=Demography |publisher=Duke University Press |volume=5 |issue=1 |date=1968-03-01 |issn=0070-3370 |doi=10.1007/bf03208583 |pages=382–409 |s2cid=46970216 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

{{Cquote|Whenever I meet in [[Pierre-Simon Laplace|Laplace]] with the words "Thus it plainly appears," I am sure that hours, and perhaps days, of hard study will alone enable me to discover how it plainly appears.
| author = [[Nathaniel Bowditch]]
| source = Memoir of Nathaniel Bowditch (1839) p. 62.
}}

In a memoir, [[Gian-Carlo Rota]] claimed that the expression "proof by intimidation" was coined by [[Mark Kac]], to describe a technique used by [[William Feller]] in his lectures:
{{Cquote|He took umbrage when someone interrupted his lecturing by pointing out some glaring mistake. He became red in the face and raised his voice, often to full shouting range. It was reported that on occasion he had asked the objector to leave the classroom. The expression "proof by intimidation" was coined after Feller's lectures (by Mark Kac). During a Feller lecture, the hearer was made to feel privy to some wondrous secret, one that often vanished by magic as he walked out of the classroom at the end of the period. Like many great teachers, Feller was a bit of a con man.
| author = 
| source = {{Cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/indiscretethough0000rota |title=Indiscrete thoughts |last=Rota |first=Gian-Carlo |date=1997 |publisher=Birkhäuser |others=Palombi, Fabrizio, 1965– |isbn=0-8176-3866-0 |location=Boston |oclc=34029702 |url-access=registration}}
}}{{Cquote|Newton's astonishing grasp of the entire problem of planetary perturbations and the power of his insight are clearly apparent, this part of the Principia is also among the most difficult to grasp because of the paucity of any real explanation and an apparent attempt to conceal details by recourse, too often, to phrases like "hence it comes to pass", "by like reasoning", and "it is manifest that" at crucial points of the argument. This "secretive style" is nowhere present, to the same extent, in the Principia.
|author = [[Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar]]
|source = {{Cite book |last=Chandrasekhar |first=S. |title=Newton's Principia for the common reader |date=1995 |publisher=Clarendon Press; Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-851744-3 |location=Oxford: Oxford; New York |page=258}}
}}
